title: Optimizing LLMs in Insurance with DSPy: Jeronim Morina

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on DSPy for automated prompt optimization and modular LLM programming patterns, directly matching the prompting_llm_programming inclusion criteria and DSPy example topic. The use case is a customer-facing insurance chatbot at AXA Germany, fitting enterprise operations and its customer support sub-domain. The talk covers manual prompt prototyping, evaluation dataset construction, and DSPy-based optimization of prompts and weights. The content covers DSPy internals, evaluation methodology, and custom metric design, requiring familiarity with LLM programming concepts. This is a recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are graded 'said_in_transcript' and the talk is based on the speaker's practical experience at AXA Germany.

summary: Jeronim Morina, a machine learning engineer at AXA Germany, provocatively argues AI engineers are 'bad' because they over-focus on tools and toy datasets rather than solving real problems. He advocates first-principles engineering thinking, treating LLM applications as systems rather than just prompts. AXA is a data-driven insurance company with over 100 billion euro revenue that started a data innovation lab in 2017, built a secure internal GPT platform on Azure with OpenAI in 2023, and announced a Mistral AI collaboration. He contrasts large insurers as slow 'ice breakers' versus Silicon Valley 'speedboats.' The core example is a customer-facing chatbot for navigating insurance terms and conditions. Manual prompt engineering proved error-prone, sensitive to minor changes, and produced fragile systems with excessive error-handling code. Morina strongly recommends inspecting what prompt-engineering tools actually send to LLMs using mitm proxy, citing Ham Hussein's blog posts, and using Arize Phoenix for tracing. He stresses building proper evaluation datasets with clean input-output pairs while avoiding data leakage. Only after establishing this baseline did they try DSPy, which he describes using a neural-network analogy: define modules in __init__ (like PyTorch layers) and describe execution flow in forward(). DSPy compiles programs into different instructions via few-shot prompting and fine-tuning, using a metric to optimize. Key learnings include that standard metrics like exact match and passage match only work for English—German requires custom metrics and evaluators. DSPy's typed modules may need custom extensions. They confirmed one big monolithic model does not work. Final takeaways: write prompts by hand first to prove achievability, start with basic evaluations (regex, string comparisons) before LLM-as-judge, don't over-complicate, and make small adjustments. Morina closes by recommending Conor Shorton's DSPy learning resources and encouraging attendees to find meaningful problems solvable with AI.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: We Are All Bad AI Engineers
sections.summary: Morina provocatively argues AI engineers are 'bad' because they over-focus on tools and toy problems like hotpot QA datasets instead of solving real problems. He calls for returning to first-principles engineering and treating LLMs as systems rather than standalone models.

sections.title: AXA Context and Insurance Industry Challenges
sections.summary: AXA is a data-focused insurance company with over 100 billion euro revenue. Climate change drives increasing claims and labor. AXA Germany's data innovation lab started in 2017 works cross-collaboratively with business units. They built a secure GPT platform on Azure with OpenAI in 2023 and announced Mistral AI collaboration.

sections.title: Example Problem and Prompt Engineering Challenges
sections.summary: The example use case is a customer-facing chatbot for navigating insurance terms and conditions. The team worked with domain experts to craft about a dozen examples. Manual prompt engineering proved to be 'black magic'—hard, error-prone, with hardcoded templates and intransparent usage. Sensitivity to minor prompt changes caused major issues.

sections.title: First Principles: Inspect What Tools Actually Send
sections.summary: Morina strongly advocates inspecting what prompt-engineering tools actually send to LLMs, recommending Ham Hussein's blog post and using mitm proxy. He warns against the trap that 'these tools will solve the problem for me' and insists on first-principles thinking.

sections.title: Observability with Arize Phoenix
sections.summary: The team used Arize Phoenix open-source library for tracing and observability to understand which calls are bundled together and what happens behind the curtains in their LLM chains. This was essential before any optimization.

sections.title: Evaluations and Data Preparation
sections.summary: Morina stresses the need for proper evaluations beyond 'looks good to me at 10.' Data preparation took several months. Critical warning about data leakage: ensure output labels cannot be deduced from input data. Recommends Ham Hussein's blog post on evals.

sections.title: DSPy Adoption and Modular Decomposition
sections.summary: Morina encountered DSPy through meeting Omar at Scale AI Bay in November. DSPy has a steep learning curve and is not a blanket recommendation. Key requirement: decompose problems into separate modules (retrieval, multi-hop QA, etc.) rather than building one huge ReAct prompt, so DSPy can optimize each module.

sections.title: DSPy Optimizers and Neural Network Analogy
sections.summary: DSPy adds optimizers that tune prompts and weights given a metric—here, finding the right answer. DSPy compiles the same program into different instructions via few-shot prompting and fine-tuning. Morina draws an analogy to PyTorch: define modules like Chain of Thought or ReAct in __init__ (like convolution/dropout layers), then describe retrieval and other operations in the forward path.

sections.title: Key Learnings: German Language Metrics and Custom Modules
sections.summary: For German text, standard metrics like exact match and passage match only work for English—custom metrics are needed. DSPy's typed modules (typed predictor, typed Chain of Thought) may not fit specific use cases, requiring custom modules. Evaluation is also fixed on English, so custom evaluators are needed for German. They confirmed one big monolithic model does not work.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Start Simple and Measure
sections.summary: Morina lists final takeaways: write prompts by hand first to prove the task is achievable; you can't improve what you don't measure; avoid 'looks good to me' metrics without annotated data; start with basic evaluations like regex and string comparisons before using LLM-as-judge; don't over-complicate; make very small adjustments.

sections.title: Closing: Spark Curiosity and Find Good Problems
sections.summary: Morina acknowledges a 20-minute talk can't teach DSPy fully. He recommends learning resources from Conor Shorton and the DSPy website. His goal was to spark curiosity and interest, encouraging attendees to become better AI engineers through first-principles thinking and to find meaningful problems worth solving with AI.
